newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: NORMAL RAINS SEEN FILLING SOUTHERN AFRICA CROPS.
newsitem.headline: NORMAL RAINS SEEN FILLING SOUTHERN AFRICA CROPS.

text.p: Long-term weather forecasts for southern Africa indicate a normal 1996/97 summer rainfall season with promising outlooks for the region's crops, weather experts said on Wednesday.
Good rains -- vital for the economies of the southern cone of Africa -- are expected in the region from December, although rainfall could be slow to get started in some areas, they said.
The region experienced its best rains in years last season, boosting output of staple foodstuffs sharply.

The Climate and Weather Research Laboratory at the University of Cape Town said in its latest seasonal outlook that climatic signals for 1996/97 summer rainfall were increasingly favourable in October.
"Near average rains may be expected. Results indicate good rainfall and high maize yields over the Free State and Eastern Cape of South Africa," the outlook said.
It added that rainfall models indicated a shift in rainfall to late summer.

It said positive features for the region's long-term weather outlook were average or slightly cooler than average (La Nina) wind circulations over Indonesia, below normal tropical eastern Pacific sea temperatures and positive air pressure anomolies south of the African continent.
South Africa's National Maize Producers Organisation (Nampo) said last week that conditions looked favourable for the 1997 crop which farmers were in the early stages of planting.
"At this stage conditions are looking very good," Nampo economist Andre Ferreira said, adding that long-term weather forecasts indicated that the industry could expect a good crop.
"If you couple this to good moisture status then it seems as if we can expect a reasonably good crop."

University of Cape Town Oceanography Department director Mark Jury told Reuters his maize yield models indicated a South African crop about 17 percent above normal, although Zimbabwe's crop could drop as much as 31 percent below normal.
South Africa's main maize-growing area, the Free State province, could expect a crop 51 percent above normal, mainly due to the La Nina influence, Jury said.
"What the maize yield model is showing is that there is a gradient that goes from northeast from southwest.
"From Zimbabwe, which is below normal, to the Northern Province, which is probably near normal to the Gauteng region which is above normal to the Free State which is well above normal.
"My model seem to be indicating that there is going to be slightly below normal maize yields to the northeast and as you move to the southwest, maize yields should increase," he said.
South Africa's National Crop Estimates Committee puts this year's maize crop at 9.48 million tonnes, up from the 4.41 million in the previous year.
In neigbouring Zimbabwe, Meteorological Office officials said the country could expect normal rains.
Rains at the weekend marked the beginning of the season and farmers have been urged to start planting.
"The rains heralded the start of the rain season and farmers should take advantage and go ahead with their planting as the conditions are favourable," one official said.

The Zimbabwe Tobacco Association said it was encouraging its members to aim for increased production of tobacco -- the main agricultural export -- from 119 million kg in 1996 to 230 million kg next year.
Zimbabwe's 1996/1997 maize crop has been forecast at around 2.8 million tonnes, the same as in the previous season.
Production of seed cotton, another key export, was expected to increase to 300,000 tonnes from the 285,000 tonnes in the previous season.
